title: Lucky Seven 4 Massachusetts

lines.speaker: CHAP
lines.visual: card:Chapter Four · Massachusetts|James Sullivan · Harvard's state

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Worcester County, Massachusetts. 1781. A Black man named Quock Walker leaves the farm of the man who claims to own him. The man, Nathaniel Jennison, catches him and beats him.
lines.caption: Worcester County, Massachusetts. 1781. A Black man named Quock Walker leaves the farm of the man who claims to own him. The man, Nathaniel Jennison, catches him and beats him.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Walker sues. A jury declares him a free man. And the cases that follow help end slavery in Massachusetts, without a single law ever being passed to do it.
lines.caption: Walker sues. A jury declares him a free man. And the cases that follow help end slavery in Massachusetts, without a single law ever being passed to do it.
lines.visual: card:The Quock Walker cases|Worcester County, 1781 to 1783

lines.speaker: HA
lines.say: Crimson, the floor is mine. And this is the part of Massachusetts history we should lead with, every time.
lines.caption: Crimson, the floor is mine. And this is the part of Massachusetts history we should lead with, every time.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: I thought slavery was a Southern thing.
lines.caption: I thought slavery was a Southern thing.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: It was a Massachusetts thing too, Gary. In the criminal case against Jennison, one of the judges at the preliminary hearing was the man who'd become our seventh governor. James Sullivan.
lines.caption: It was a Massachusetts thing too, Gary. In the criminal case against Jennison, one of the judges at the preliminary hearing was the man who'd become our seventh governor. James Sullivan.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: James Sullivan was born April 22nd, 1744, in Berwick, in the part of Massachusetts that's now Maine. He never went to college.
lines.caption: James Sullivan was born April 22nd, 1744, in Berwick, in the part of Massachusetts that's now Maine. He never went to college.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: As a boy he hurt his foot badly, and while he was laid up, he taught himself Latin and the classics at home. Then he studied law under his older brother, John.
lines.caption: As a boy he hurt his foot badly, and while he was laid up, he taught himself Latin and the classics at home. Then he studied law under his older brother, John.
lines.visual: card:Fact 1 of 7|Self-taught at home after a childhood injury · no college

lines.speaker: HA
lines.say: No Harvard seat. And yet he outworked half the men who had one.
lines.caption: No Harvard seat. And yet he outworked half the men who had one.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: In March 1776 he joined the Superior Court of Judicature, the colony's highest court, soon to be the state's. He resigned in 1782 in a fight over salary.
lines.caption: In March 1776 he joined the Superior Court of Judicature, the colony's highest court, soon to be the state's. He resigned in 1782 in a fight over salary.
lines.visual: card:Fact 2 of 7|A judge on the state's highest court, 1776 to 1782

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: The Walker cases weren't alone. In August 1781, in Great Barrington, an enslaved woman named Bett and a man named Brom sued for their freedom under the new state constitution, which said all men are born free and equal. The jury freed them and awarded thirty shillings. She took the name Elizabeth Freeman.
lines.caption: The Walker cases weren't alone. In August 1781, in Great Barrington, an enslaved woman named Bett and a man named Brom sued for their freedom under the new state constitution, which said all men are born free and equal. The jury freed them and awarded thirty shillings. She took the name Elizabeth Freeman.

lines.speaker: HA
lines.say: Elizabeth Freeman. Remember the name, because she didn't wait for anybody to hand it to her.
lines.caption: Elizabeth Freeman. Remember the name, because she didn't wait for anybody to hand it to her.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Quock Walker's own civil suit ended with a jury calling him a free man and awarding him fifty pounds. The constitution of 1780 was never amended to ban slavery outright. The courts and the people who sued did the work.
lines.caption: Quock Walker's own civil suit ended with a jury calling him a free man and awarding him fifty pounds. The constitution of 1780 was never amended to ban slavery outright. The courts and the people who sued did the work.
lines.visual: card:Massachusetts, 1780 to 1783|No law ended slavery · lawsuits did

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He publicly opposed slavery. While Walker's lawyers, Levi Lincoln and Caleb Strong, argued the civil cases, the criminal case climbed to the top court. In April 1783, Chief Justice William Cushing told the jury that slavery was, in his judgment, as effectively abolished as it can be. Jennison was convicted and fined forty shillings.
lines.caption: He publicly opposed slavery. While Walker's lawyers, Levi Lincoln and Caleb Strong, argued the civil cases, the criminal case climbed to the top court. In April 1783, Chief Justice William Cushing told the jury that slavery was, in his judgment, as effectively abolished as it can be. Jennison was convicted and fined forty shillings.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: By the 1790 census, Massachusetts reported no enslaved people at all.
lines.caption: By the 1790 census, Massachusetts reported no enslaved people at all.
lines.visual: card:Fact 3 of 7|By the 1790 census, Massachusetts reported no enslaved people

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: In 1787, after Shays' Rebellion, the armed uprising in western Massachusetts, Sullivan helped defend men charged in it, and the government's lawyers criticized him for it.
lines.caption: In 1787, after Shays' Rebellion, the armed uprising in western Massachusetts, Sullivan helped defend men charged in it, and the government's lawyers criticized him for it.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: From 1790 to 1807 he served as attorney general of Massachusetts.
lines.caption: From 1790 to 1807 he served as attorney general of Massachusetts.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: So he's a judge, he's against slavery, he defends the rebels. When does he become governor?
lines.caption: So he's a judge, he's against slavery, he defends the rebels. When does he become governor?

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Not for a while. He ran for governor and lost in 1797. Lost in 1798. Lost in 1805. Lost in 1806. Four straight defeats.
lines.caption: Not for a while. He ran for governor and lost in 1797. Lost in 1798. Lost in 1805. Lost in 1806. Four straight defeats.
lines.visual: card:Fact 4 of 7|He lost four races for governor before he won in 1807

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: In 1807 he finally won. He's the seventh governor because Massachusetts gives a new number every time someone comes back. John Hancock served twice, so he is number one and number three.
lines.caption: In 1807 he finally won. He's the seventh governor because Massachusetts gives a new number every time someone comes back. John Hancock served twice, so he is number one and number three.

lines.speaker: HA
lines.say: And if you count each man once, Hancock only takes one slot, and number seven becomes Christopher Gore. Hold that thought.
lines.caption: And if you count each man once, Hancock only takes one slot, and number seven becomes Christopher Gore. Hold that thought.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Sullivan took office May 29th, 1807. He founded the Massachusetts Historical Society as its first president, and he was a major force behind the Middlesex Canal, which linked the Merrimack River to Boston.
lines.caption: Sullivan took office May 29th, 1807. He founded the Massachusetts Historical Society as its first president, and he was a major force behind the Middlesex Canal, which linked the Merrimack River to Boston.
lines.visual: card:Fact 5 of 7|Founding president of the Massachusetts Historical Society · champion of the Middlesex Canal

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: But his time in the governor's chair was short. James Sullivan died in office on December 10th, 1808, after about eighteen months.
lines.caption: But his time in the governor's chair was short. James Sullivan died in office on December 10th, 1808, after about eighteen months.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Sullivan's public life went beyond the courtroom. In 1796 he served as the American agent on the commission that fixed the border between Maine and New Brunswick at the St. Croix River. He wrote a history of the District of Maine in 1795, and a history of land titles in Massachusetts in 1801.
lines.caption: Sullivan's public life went beyond the courtroom. In 1796 he served as the American agent on the commission that fixed the border between Maine and New Brunswick at the St. Croix River. He wrote a history of the District of Maine in 1795, and a history of land titles in Massachusetts in 1801.
lines.visual: card:James Sullivan, historian|The History of the District of Maine, 1795

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: A guy who lost four elections and still found time to write two history books. I can't finish a crossword.
lines.caption: A guy who lost four elections and still found time to write two history books. I can't finish a crossword.

lines.speaker: HA
lines.say: Some of us lose elections, Gary. Some of us lose crosswords.
lines.caption: Some of us lose elections, Gary. Some of us lose crosswords.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Now, the man waiting at number eight. Christopher Gore. Harvard class of 1776. One of the richest lawyers in the country.
lines.caption: Now, the man waiting at number eight. Christopher Gore. Harvard class of 1776. One of the richest lawyers in the country.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Continental soldiers had often been paid in paper, and many of them sold it at a steep discount just to get by. Gore bought it. One batch cost him about thirty-seven hundred dollars for twenty-five thousand dollars face value.
lines.caption: Continental soldiers had often been paid in paper, and many of them sold it at a steep discount just to get by. Gore bought it. One batch cost him about thirty-seven hundred dollars for twenty-five thousand dollars face value.
lines.visual: card:Fact 6 of 7|Gore bought soldiers' war paper at a steep discount

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Then in 1790, Congress, on Alexander Hamilton's plan, made that paper good at face value. The soldiers had sold low. The buyer cashed in.
lines.caption: Then in 1790, Congress, on Alexander Hamilton's plan, made that paper good at face value. The soldiers had sold low. The buyer cashed in.

lines.speaker: G
lines.say: So the guys who fought the war sold their pay for pennies, and the lawyer got rich off it.
lines.caption: So the guys who fought the war sold their pay for pennies, and the lawyer got rich off it.

lines.speaker: HA
lines.say: That's the story, Gary. Harvard named its first library after him. Gore Hall, 1838.
lines.caption: That's the story, Gary. Harvard named its first library after him. Gore Hall, 1838.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Gore had been the first United States Attorney for Massachusetts, appointed in 1789. He spent years in London on a Jay Treaty commission. In 1807 he defended a young lawyer named Thomas Selfridge, who had shot a man named Charles Austin on a Boston street. The foreman of the jury was Paul Revere. It took about fifteen minutes to acquit.
lines.caption: Gore had been the first United States Attorney for Massachusetts, appointed in 1789. He spent years in London on a Jay Treaty commission. In 1807 he defended a young lawyer named Thomas Selfridge, who had shot a man named Charles Austin on a Boston street. The foreman of the jury was Paul Revere. It took about fifteen minutes to acquit.
lines.visual: card:Commonwealth v. Selfridge, 1807|Gore for the defense · Paul Revere, foreman · acquitted

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: He served one year as governor, 1809 to 1810, then lost to Elbridge Gerry. He went to the U.S. Senate in 1813 and opposed the War of 1812. A young Daniel Webster studied law in his office. Gore Hall stood at Harvard until 1915, when it was torn down to make room for Widener Library.
lines.caption: He served one year as governor, 1809 to 1810, then lost to Elbridge Gerry. He went to the U.S. Senate in 1813 and opposed the War of 1812. A young Daniel Webster studied law in his office. Gore Hall stood at Harvard until 1915, when it was torn down to make room for Widener Library.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Gore lived grandly at his country estate, Gore Place in Waltham, now a National Historic Landmark. Sullivan took the long road. Four losses, one win, and a grave.
lines.caption: Gore lived grandly at his country estate, Gore Place in Waltham, now a National Historic Landmark. Sullivan took the long road. Four losses, one win, and a grave.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: James Sullivan is buried in Boston's Granary Burying Ground, in a tomb he shares with a colonial governor, Richard Bellingham. Sullivan Square in Charlestown carries his name. And Harvard gave him an honorary degree in 1779.
lines.caption: James Sullivan is buried in Boston's Granary Burying Ground, in a tomb he shares with a colonial governor, Richard Bellingham. Sullivan Square in Charlestown carries his name. And Harvard gave him an honorary degree in 1779.
lines.visual: card:Fact 7 of 7|Sullivan Square is named for him · buried in the Granary Burying Ground

lines.speaker: HA
lines.say: Veritas. And the truth here is that the courts moved faster than the lawmakers did. Ashworth out.
lines.caption: Veritas. And the truth here is that the courts moved faster than the lawmakers did. Ashworth out.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Four losses before a win. His side of history took a lot longer.
lines.caption: Four losses before a win. His side of history took a lot longer.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: So, Massachusetts. Your lucky seven, one more time.
lines.caption: So, Massachusetts. Your lucky seven, one more time.

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: One. Self-taught at home after a childhood injury. No college.
lines.caption: One. Self-taught at home after a childhood injury. No college.
lines.visual: card:One|Self-taught at home after a childhood injury · no college

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Two. A judge on the state's highest court, 1776 to 1782.
lines.caption: Two. A judge on the state's highest court, 1776 to 1782.
lines.visual: card:Two|A judge on the state's highest court, 1776 to 1782

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Three. By the 1790 census, Massachusetts reported no enslaved people.
lines.caption: Three. By the 1790 census, Massachusetts reported no enslaved people.
lines.visual: card:Three|By the 1790 census, Massachusetts reported no enslaved people

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Four. He lost four races for governor before he won in 1807.
lines.caption: Four. He lost four races for governor before he won in 1807.
lines.visual: card:Four|He lost four races for governor before he won in 1807

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Five. Founding president of the Massachusetts Historical Society. Champion of the Middlesex Canal.
lines.caption: Five. Founding president of the Massachusetts Historical Society. Champion of the Middlesex Canal.
lines.visual: card:Five|Founding president of the Massachusetts Historical Society · champion of the Middlesex Canal

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Six. Gore bought soldiers' war paper at a steep discount.
lines.caption: Six. Gore bought soldiers' war paper at a steep discount.
lines.visual: card:Six|Gore bought soldiers' war paper at a steep discount

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Seven. Sullivan Square is named for him. Buried in the Granary Burying Ground.
lines.caption: Seven. Sullivan Square is named for him. Buried in the Granary Burying Ground.
lines.visual: card:Seven|Sullivan Square is named for him · buried in the Granary Burying Ground

lines.speaker: M
lines.say: Massachusetts. Keep it real.
lines.caption: Massachusetts. Keep it real.
